mcqs.q: Primary dentin consists of:
mcqs.explain: Primary dentin (formed before root completion) comprises mantle dentin and circumpulpal dentin.

mcqs.q: Secondary dentin is best described as:
opts: Physiologic dentin formed slowly over the whole pulpal surface after root completion
mcqs.explain: Secondary dentin is laid down physiologically (not from trauma) over the entire pulpal surface after root formation, at a slower rate.

mcqs.q: Secondary dentin deposition results in:
opts: Pulp recession (smaller pulp cavity, obliterated pulp horns)
mcqs.explain: Secondary dentin reduces the size of the pulp cavity and obliterates the pulp horns (pulp recession); its tubules are wavier and fewer.

mcqs.q: Reactionary (response) tertiary dentin forms when:
opts: A mild stimulus occurs and the original odontoblasts survive
An aggressive stimulus kills the odontoblasts
mcqs.explain: Reactionary dentin forms in a localized area in response to a mild stimulus that does NOT damage the odontoblasts; its tubules are irregular.

mcqs.q: Reparative dentin forms when:
opts: An aggressive stimulus kills the odontoblasts, and subodontoblastic UMCs differentiate to replace them
A mild stimulus leaves odontoblasts intact
mcqs.explain: An aggressive stimulus degenerates the odontoblasts; undifferentiated mesenchymal cells from the subodontoblastic layer differentiate to form heterogeneous reparative dentin.

mcqs.q: Which is a recognised type of reparative dentin?
mcqs.explain: Reparative dentin is heterogeneous and may be atubular dentin, osteodentin (entrapped cells) or vasodentin (entrapped blood vessels).

mcqs.q: 'Vasodentin' refers to reparative dentin containing:
mcqs.explain: Vasodentin is reparative dentin with entrapped blood vessels; osteodentin has entrapped cells, and atubular dentin lacks tubules.

mcqs.q: Why does pulp recession (from secondary dentin) help during cavity preparation?
opts: It makes pulp exposure less likely in older patients
mcqs.explain: The smaller pulp chamber and obliterated pulp horns make pulp exposure during cavity preparation less likely in older patients.

mcqs.q: Tertiary (localized) dentin formation in response to caries acts as a:
opts: Barrier that increases the time for caries to reach the pulp
mcqs.explain: The localized tertiary dentin acts as a barrier, increasing the time caries takes to reach the pulp.

mcqs.q: Pulp capping is possible because of the property of:
mcqs.explain: Because the pulp can form reparative dentin, pulp capping can be used to protect/heal an exposed or nearly exposed pulp.

mcqs.q: Cavity preparation in YOUNG patients carries a greater risk of:
opts: Exposing the pulp (the pulp chamber is larger)
mcqs.explain: Young patients have larger pulp chambers (less secondary dentin), so cavity preparation more easily exposes the pulp.

mcqs.q: Transparent (sclerotic) dentin forms when a mild stimulus causes:
opts: Calcification/occlusion of the dentinal tubules, giving a uniform refractive index
mcqs.explain: Mild stimulation causes odontoblast fatty degeneration then tubular calcification/occlusion; the uniform refractive index makes the area translucent (transparent dentin).

mcqs.q: Sclerotic dentin appears ___ by transmitted light:
mcqs.explain: Because the occluded tubules give a uniform refractive index, sclerotic dentin appears translucent by transmitted light.

mcqs.q: Dead tracts result from a SEVERE stimulus and appear:
opts: Black (empty, wide dentinal tubules) by transmitted light
mcqs.explain: Severe stimulation destroys the odontoblastic process/odontoblasts, leaving empty wide tubules that appear black by transmitted light.

mcqs.q: Beneath a dead tract (from the pulpal surface), there is usually:
opts: Reparative dentin (with sclerotic dentin surrounding the tract)
mcqs.explain: Reparative dentin forms beneath dead tracts, and the dead tract is surrounded by sclerotic dentin.

mcqs.q: The nerve plexus in the subodontoblastic layer of the pulp is the:
mcqs.explain: The plexus of Raschkow lies in the subodontoblastic layer; its nerves lose their Schwann sheath and enter the dentinal tubules.

mcqs.q: Dentin is MOST sensitive at the:
opts: DEJ and near the pulpal surface
mcqs.explain: Dentin sensitivity is highest at the DEJ (profuse tubule branching) and near the pulpal surface; the middle is less sensitive.

mcqs.q: The MOST ACCEPTED theory of dentin sensitivity is the:
mcqs.explain: The hydrodynamic theory is the most accepted: a stimulus moves fluid within the tubule, which is registered by pulpal free nerve endings near the odontoblasts.

mcqs.q: Evidence AGAINST the direct neural stimulation theory includes:
opts: Absence of nerve fibres in the outer (DEJ) dentin, the most sensitive region
Local anaesthetic on dentin abolishing sensitivity
mcqs.explain: Against direct neural stimulation: nerves are absent in the most sensitive outer dentin (DEJ), and surface LA does not abolish sensitivity.

mcqs.q: The increased sensitivity at the DEJ is explained by:
opts: Profuse branching of the dentinal tubules in this region
mcqs.explain: The profuse branching (terminal plexus) of the dentinal tubules at the DEJ explains the increased sensitivity there (hydrodynamic theory).

mcqs.q: Compared with primary dentin, the dentinal tubules of secondary dentin are:
opts: Fewer and follow a more wavy course
mcqs.explain: Secondary dentin tubules change direction to a more wavy course and are fewer in number.

mcqs.q: An odontoblast undergoing the first step toward sclerotic dentin shows:
opts: Fatty degeneration of the cell and its process
mcqs.explain: In sclerotic dentin formation, the odontoblast and its process first undergo fatty degeneration, followed by tubular calcification and occlusion.

saqs.a: Primary (mantle + circumpulpal), secondary (physiologic, after root completion), tertiary (reactionary or reparative), plus predentin.

saqs.q: Describe secondary dentin and its clinical effect.
saqs.a: Physiologic dentin laid slowly over the whole pulpal surface after root completion; tubules are wavier and fewer. It causes pulp recession (smaller chamber, obliterated horns) → less risk of pulp exposure.

saqs.q: Contrast reactionary and reparative tertiary dentin.
saqs.a: Reactionary: mild stimulus, original odontoblasts survive. Reparative: aggressive stimulus kills odontoblasts, subodontoblastic UMCs replace them — may be atubular, osteodentin or vasodentin.

saqs.q: Give the clinical significance of secondary and tertiary dentin.
saqs.a: Secondary → pulp recession (less exposure during cavity prep). Tertiary → barrier delaying caries reaching the pulp and allows pulp capping. Young patients (large pulp) have higher exposure risk.

saqs.q: Contrast sclerotic dentin and dead tracts.
saqs.a: Sclerotic (transparent): mild stimulus → tubules calcify/occlude → uniform refractive index → translucent. Dead tracts: severe stimulus → empty wide tubules → appear black (reparative dentin forms beneath).
Nerves of the plexus of Raschkow (subodontoblastic) lose their Schwann sheath, pass between odontoblasts and enter the tubules (more in crown). Dentin is most sensitive at the DEJ and near the pulp.

saqs.q: Name and explain the most accepted theory of dentin sensitivity.
saqs.a: The hydrodynamic (fluid) theory: a stimulus causes fluid movement within the tubule, registered by pulpal free nerve endings; DEJ sensitivity is due to profuse tubule branching there.
